video.title: Relationships: Scatter plots and correlation
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor - the students' science teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our class asked: does sleep help our marks? We collected sleep hours and test marks for everyone in the class. Two numbers for each of us. How could we see if they go together?
Today: scatter plots, correlation, and why together is not the same as cause.

scenes.on_screen_text: A scatter plot: one dot per pupil
scenes.narration: A scatter plot puts one measurement across and the other up. Each pupil becomes one dot. Sleep goes along the bottom, and the mark goes up the side.
If the dots rise from left to right, that is a positive relationship. If they fall, it is negative, like screen time late at night and marks. If they make a shapeless cloud, there is no relationship.
The correlation, called r, measures how close the dots are to a straight line. It goes from minus one to one. Near one is a strong positive pattern, near zero is no straight-line pattern.
Here is a famous pattern. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Does ice cream make people drown? No. Hot weather brings both.
So when sleep and marks go together, ask what else could explain it. Families with calm homes may give children both more sleep and more help with homework.
Quick check! The dots lie very close to a rising straight line. Which r fits best?
About zero point nine. Rising means positive, and close to a line means strong. Minus zero point nine would be a strong falling pattern.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: scatter and best fit
scenes.narration: In the app, open Scatter, correlation and best fit. Tap to add pupils who study a lot but score low, and watch r fall.
Your turn. Pupils with more books at home get higher marks, with r of zero point six. Does that prove books cause higher marks?
No, not on its own. Remember: a scatter plot shows two measurements, r measures how close they are to a line, and correlation is not cause. Always ask what else could explain it.
Try it yourself: measure the height and arm span of five people at home, and plot them. Is there a pattern, and does one really cause the other?

checkpoints.prompt: The dots lie very close to a rising straight line. Which r fits best?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: rising and close to a line means a strong positive correlation.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: rising means positive, and close to a line means strong, so about 0.9.

checkpoints.prompt: More books at home goes with higher marks (r = 0.6). Does that prove books cause higher marks?

options.text: No: something else may explain both

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: families with more books may also give more time and help. Correlation is not cause.
